To build a stronger economy, we need to support the backbone of our city—small businesses—while fostering innovation and recruiting major employers offering career-track jobs
## Parks
Our parks are vital spaces for families, children, and seniors alike. I will launch an annual survey to ensure our parks are clean, accessible, and meeting the needs of every resident.
## Fair Share of Dollars
Fresno deserves its fair share of state and federal funding. I will work tirelessly to bring those dollars home.
## Homelessness
Homelessness requires a compassionate yet practical approach. I will foster partnerships between the city, county, nonprofits, and faith-based organizations to deliver real solutions.
## Infrastructure
Fresno’s roads, sidewalks, and infrastructure need serious attention. I will prioritize fixing potholes, modernizing our transit systems, and ensuring that every neighborhood has access to safe and reliable infrastructure.
## Sports and Entertainment
Sports and entertainment bring communities together and put cities on the map. I’ll work to bring professional soccer to Fresno, support Fresno State’s entry into the PAC-12, and advocate for expanding entertainment venues across the city. Sports can be a catalyst for economic growth and civic pride.
## A Vision for Blackstone and Manchester Mall
Manchester Mall has the potential to become Fresno’s first major mixed-use development—a vibrant space where people can live, work, shop, and play. I will work with developers, investors, and community members to turn this vision into reality, making Blackstone a corridor of opportunity for all.
## Housing
Fresno must address its housing crisis by increasing the supply of all types of housing—affordable units, starter homes, and market-rate apartments. I will streamline approval processes and work with builders to ensure we meet the needs of a growing population without sacrificing quality or sustainability.
## Engaging the Youth
Our city’s future depends on our young people. I will create initiatives to engage youth in decision-making processes, expand mentorship and internship opportunities, and support programs that inspire the next generation of Fresno leaders. Investing in our youth is investing in Fresno’s success.
## Seniors and Veterans
Our seniors and veterans have given so much to our community, and it’s time we give back. I will advocate for expanded senior services, improved healthcare access, and programs that honor and support our veterans. Ensuring dignity and opportunity for these groups is a personal priority for me.
## Constituent Services
Every resident deserves to have their voice heard. I will establish accessible office hours, improve communication channels, and ensure that every concern—big or small—is addressed promptly. My commitment is to serve as an advocate for every person in District 7 – you deserve a response from your Councilmember.
﻿
## Fiscal Responsibility
Fresno’s budget must reflect the priorities of its residents. I will ensure that every dollar spent delivers tangible results, cutting waste and increasing transparency. Fiscal responsibility isn’t just about balancing the budget—it’s about investing in our community’s future.
— Nav Gurm's campaign website (March 27, 2026)

Our city’s future depends on our young people. I will create initiatives to engage youth in decision-making processes, expand mentorship and internship opportunities, and support programs that inspire the next generation of Fresno leaders. Investing in our youth is investing in Fresno’s success.
## Seniors and Veterans
Our seniors and veterans have given so much to our community, and it’s time we give back. I will advocate for expanded senior services, improved healthcare access, and programs that honor and support our veterans. Ensuring dignity and opportunity for these groups is a personal priority for me.
## Constituent Services
Every resident deserves to have their voice heard. I will establish accessible office hours, improve communication channels, and ensure that every concern—big or small—is addressed promptly. My commitment is to serve as an advocate for every person in District 7 – you deserve a response from your Councilmember.
﻿
## Fiscal Responsibility
Fresno’s budget must reflect the priorities of its residents. I will ensure that every dollar spent delivers tangible results, cutting waste and increasing transparency. Fiscal responsibility isn’t just about balancing the budget—it’s about investing in our community’s future.
— Nav Gurm's campaign website (March 27, 2026)

#### Campaign website
Enriquez's campaign website stated the following:
# Priorities for Kerman
### Responsible Growth While Protecting Kerman's Character
Kerman has changed significantly since Yazmine moved here at age 11.
Growth can bring new businesses, families and opportunities. It also raises an important question: how does Kerman continue moving forward without losing the community character that made people proud to call it home?
Yazmine hears that concern from longtime residents, who express pride in how far Kerman has come while wanting its history and small-town identity protected.
For Yazmine, responsible growth means looking forward while understanding where Kerman came from.
### A Stronger Environment for Small Business
Yazmine knows firsthand how much work goes into opening, maintaining and growing a small business.
She has heard concerns about slow foot traffic, rising competition, permitting and the complexity of navigating requirements.
Yazmine would like to see:
- Clearer information about business requirements
- Better communication regarding application status
- Reasonable permit-processing times
- More opportunities for event-driven local commerce
- Local business owners included in conversations about Kerman's future
These priorities directly reflect the concerns she describes hearing from local business owners.
### More Opportunities for Youth
Yazmine's experiences with bullying as a young person shaped the importance she places on empathy, inclusion and ensuring young people feel seen.
Through Fruta Fresca, she regularly interacts with students and enjoys hearing about their classes, sports, projects and ambitions.
She wants Kerman's young people to have more ways to discover their interests, participate in the community, develop skills and envision a future for themselves locally.
### Families and Quality of Life
Parents have shared concerns with Yazmine about bullying, limited activities for children and families, rising living costs, employment opportunities and finding ways for young people to remain engaged.
Yazmine believes families should have opportunities to spend time together, participate in their community and create memories close to home.
### Accessible and Responsive Local Leadership
Owning a business changed the way Yazmine views local government.
She has experienced how permitting, communication, demographics, development and other local decisions can affect businesses and residents.
She believes local leaders should be accessible, responsive and willing to listen.
Her approach to leadership is straightforward: hear people out, understand the problem, gather the facts, make a decision and be willing to take responsibility for it.
### A Community Where People Participate
One thing Yazmine has learned through community involvement is that Kerman has no shortage of people who care.
Sometimes people simply don't know where to start.
She wants residents, businesses, young people, organizations and community partners to have more opportunities to participate and connect.
Because a stronger Kerman isn't something any one person builds.
It's something a community builds together.
— Yazmine Enriquez's campaign website (October 14, 2026)

#### Campaign website
Enriquez's campaign website stated the following:
# Priorities for Kerman
### Responsible Growth While Protecting Kerman's Character
Kerman has changed significantly since Yazmine moved here at age 11.
Growth can bring new businesses, families and opportunities. It also raises an important question: how does Kerman continue moving forward without losing the community character that made people proud to call it home?
Yazmine hears that concern from longtime residents, who express pride in how far Kerman has come while wanting its history and small-town identity protected.
For Yazmine, responsible growth means looking forward while understanding where Kerman came from.
### A Stronger Environment for Small Business
Yazmine knows firsthand how much work goes into opening, maintaining and growing a small business.
She has heard concerns about slow foot traffic, rising competition, permitting and the complexity of navigating requirements.
Yazmine would like to see:
- Clearer information about business requirements
- Better communication regarding application status
- Reasonable permit-processing times
- More opportunities for event-driven local commerce
- Local business owners included in conversations about Kerman's future
These priorities directly reflect the concerns she describes hearing from local business owners.
### More Opportunities for Youth
Yazmine's experiences with bullying as a young person shaped the importance she places on empathy, inclusion and ensuring young people feel seen.
Through Fruta Fresca, she regularly interacts with students and enjoys hearing about their classes, sports, projects and ambitions.
She wants Kerman's young people to have more ways to discover their interests, participate in the community, develop skills and envision a future for themselves locally.
### Families and Quality of Life
Parents have shared concerns with Yazmine about bullying, limited activities for children and families, rising living costs, employment opportunities and finding ways for young people to remain engaged.
Yazmine believes families should have opportunities to spend time together, participate in their community and create memories close to home.
### Accessible and Responsive Local Leadership
Owning a business changed the way Yazmine views local government.
She has experienced how permitting, communication, demographics, development and other local decisions can affect businesses and residents.
She believes local leaders should be accessible, responsive and willing to listen.
Her approach to leadership is straightforward: hear people out, understand the problem, gather the facts, make a decision and be willing to take responsibility for it.
### A Community Where People Participate
One thing Yazmine has learned through community involvement is that Kerman has no shortage of people who care.
Sometimes people simply don't know where to start.
She wants residents, businesses, young people, organizations and community partners to have more opportunities to participate and connect.
Because a stronger Kerman isn't something any one person builds.
It's something a community builds together.
— Yazmine Enriquez's campaign website (October 14, 2026)
Note: This text is quoted verbatim from the original source. Any inconsistencies are attributable to the original source.

# Experienced leadership rooted in resilience and real results!
Mayor Pacheco is running to ensure our community in Fresno County has safe neighborhoods, experienced leadership that puts people first, and someone who understands the importance of family values.
Learn MoreRequest a Yard Sign
## Meet Maria Pacheco
Maria Pacheco is a proven leader who has made public safety a top priority. As Mayor of Kerman, Maria has worked to secure millions of dollars for public safety, support law enforcement and first responders, and invest in safer neighborhoods and infrastructure. She understands that families, businesses, and communities can only thrive when people feel safe.
Maria brings both experience and a personal understanding of the families she serves. The daughter of farmworkers, a wife and mother of six, and Mayor of Kerman, Maria knows the value of hard work, family, and opportunity. She has dedicated her career to public service, education, and strengthening communities across Western Fresno County.
As Mayor, Maria has delivered results—securing investments for public safety and parks, expanding workforce and educational opportunities, and building partnerships across communities to get things done.
Now Maria is running for Fresno County Supervisor to bring that same experienced, hands-on leadership to the county—keeping our communities safe, strengthening our economy, improving roads and infrastructure, expanding access to housing and opportunity, and making sure Western Fresno County families have a strong voice at the County.
Learn More →
Support Our Campaign
## Donate Now to Maria Pacheco for County Supervisor
$10$25$50$100$250Other
Maria’s Plan to Deliver for West Fresno County
## Priorities
### Keep Our Communities Safe
- Put more deputies on the streets and fight for the resources law enforcement needs to respond quickly and keep our community and families safe.
- Strengthen fire and emergency response, particularly in rural communities where response times can be longer.
- Expand crisis-response teams so trained professionals can handle appropriate mental-health calls and allow deputies to focus on serious crime.
- Invest in prevention and youth programs that provide after-school activities, mentorship, job training, and alternatives to gangs and crime.
### Grow Our Local Economy & Create Good Jobs
- Bring more county resources directly to West Fresno County to help small businesses grow and create local jobs.
- Expand workforce training and apprenticeships in agriculture, construction, health care, skilled trades, and emerging industries.
- Partner with Fresno State, community colleges, employers, and labor to connect residents with training for good-paying careers.
- Invest in roads, water, broadband, and infrastructure that attract businesses and allow rural communities to compete for new investment.
### Make Housing More Affordable
- Cut unnecessary delays and streamline permitting for starter homes, ADUs, modular housing, and other affordable housing options.
- Invest in water and sewer infrastructure so communities can build the housing working families need.
- Protect renters, seniors, and mobile-home residents from displacement while expanding the overall housing supply.
- Promote pathways to homeownership so more working families can build financial security and put down roots in West Fresno County.
### Protect Farming, Water & Farm Jobs
- Fight for a reliable water supply for farmers, farmworkers, families, and rural communities.
- Protect agriculture from policies that threaten local farms and jobs and make sure West Fresno County has a strong voice in county and state decisions.
- Support family farms and agricultural businesses by improving infrastructure and cutting unnecessary red tape.
- Prepare the next generation for agriculture by expanding training in ag-tech, water management, equipment, and other modern agricultural careers.

Who are you? Tell us about yourself.
Husband, Father, Outdoorsman, Amature Horticulturist, and I have helped to run a small business in our rural community for 10+ years.
Please list below 3 key messages of your campaign. What are the main points you want voters to remember about your goals for your time in office?
- Honest and Loyal. 2 qualites that should be expected of, and found in, those who run for public office.
- Compromise is Key. Compromise is essential to the future of Kerman. Without compromise, we cannot grow together in a healthy manner.
- Unity in Community. A united community is healthy community. Working together helps keep Kerman an amazing place to live, build a business, and grow a family.
What areas of public policy are you personally passionate about?
Small business growth. Kerman has had a boom in population, but small business growth has not been proportionate. Making it easier to start a small business helps our community and economy twofold by giving our residents an opportunity to build a business; offering goods and services to their neighbors, while allowing residents to buy local here in Kerman instead of going into Fresno.

#### Campaign website
Enriquez's campaign website stated the following:
# Priorities for Kerman
### Responsible Growth While Protecting Kerman's Character
Kerman has changed significantly since Yazmine moved here at age 11.
Growth can bring new businesses, families and opportunities. It also raises an important question: how does Kerman continue moving forward without losing the community character that made people proud to call it home?
Yazmine hears that concern from longtime residents, who express pride in how far Kerman has come while wanting its history and small-town identity protected.
For Yazmine, responsible growth means looking forward while understanding where Kerman came from.
### A Stronger Environment for Small Business
Yazmine knows firsthand how much work goes into opening, maintaining and growing a small business.
She has heard concerns about slow foot traffic, rising competition, permitting and the complexity of navigating requirements.
Yazmine would like to see:
- Clearer information about business requirements
- Better communication regarding application status
- Reasonable permit-processing times
- More opportunities for event-driven local commerce
- Local business owners included in conversations about Kerman's future
These priorities directly reflect the concerns she describes hearing from local business owners.
### More Opportunities for Youth
Yazmine's experiences with bullying as a young person shaped the importance she places on empathy, inclusion and ensuring young people feel seen.
Through Fruta Fresca, she regularly interacts with students and enjoys hearing about their classes, sports, projects and ambitions.
She wants Kerman's young people to have more ways to discover their interests, participate in the community, develop skills and envision a future for themselves locally.
### Families and Quality of Life
Parents have shared concerns with Yazmine about bullying, limited activities for children and families, rising living costs, employment opportunities and finding ways for young people to remain engaged.
Yazmine believes families should have opportunities to spend time together, participate in their community and create memories close to home.
### Accessible and Responsive Local Leadership
Owning a business changed the way Yazmine views local government.
She has experienced how permitting, communication, demographics, development and other local decisions can affect businesses and residents.
She believes local leaders should be accessible, responsive and willing to listen.
Her approach to leadership is straightforward: hear people out, understand the problem, gather the facts, make a decision and be willing to take responsibility for it.
### A Community Where People Participate
One thing Yazmine has learned through community involvement is that Kerman has no shortage of people who care.
Sometimes people simply don't know where to start.
She wants residents, businesses, young people, organizations and community partners to have more opportunities to participate and connect.
Because a stronger Kerman isn't something any one person builds.
It's something a community builds together.
— Yazmine Enriquez's campaign website (October 14, 2026)

# Experienced leadership rooted in resilience and real results!
Mayor Pacheco is running to ensure our community in Fresno County has safe neighborhoods, experienced leadership that puts people first, and someone who understands the importance of family values.
Learn MoreRequest a Yard Sign
## Meet Maria Pacheco
Maria Pacheco is a proven leader who has made public safety a top priority. As Mayor of Kerman, Maria has worked to secure millions of dollars for public safety, support law enforcement and first responders, and invest in safer neighborhoods and infrastructure. She understands that families, businesses, and communities can only thrive when people feel safe.
Maria brings both experience and a personal understanding of the families she serves. The daughter of farmworkers, a wife and mother of six, and Mayor of Kerman, Maria knows the value of hard work, family, and opportunity. She has dedicated her career to public service, education, and strengthening communities across Western Fresno County.
As Mayor, Maria has delivered results—securing investments for public safety and parks, expanding workforce and educational opportunities, and building partnerships across communities to get things done.
Now Maria is running for Fresno County Supervisor to bring that same experienced, hands-on leadership to the county—keeping our communities safe, strengthening our economy, improving roads and infrastructure, expanding access to housing and opportunity, and making sure Western Fresno County families have a strong voice at the County.
Learn More →
Support Our Campaign
## Donate Now to Maria Pacheco for County Supervisor
$10$25$50$100$250Other
Maria’s Plan to Deliver for West Fresno County
## Priorities
### Keep Our Communities Safe
- Put more deputies on the streets and fight for the resources law enforcement needs to respond quickly and keep our community and families safe.
- Strengthen fire and emergency response, particularly in rural communities where response times can be longer.
- Expand crisis-response teams so trained professionals can handle appropriate mental-health calls and allow deputies to focus on serious crime.
- Invest in prevention and youth programs that provide after-school activities, mentorship, job training, and alternatives to gangs and crime.
### Grow Our Local Economy & Create Good Jobs
- Bring more county resources directly to West Fresno County to help small businesses grow and create local jobs.
- Expand workforce training and apprenticeships in agriculture, construction, health care, skilled trades, and emerging industries.
- Partner with Fresno State, community colleges, employers, and labor to connect residents with training for good-paying careers.
- Invest in roads, water, broadband, and infrastructure that attract businesses and allow rural communities to compete for new investment.
### Make Housing More Affordable
- Cut unnecessary delays and streamline permitting for starter homes, ADUs, modular housing, and other affordable housing options.
- Invest in water and sewer infrastructure so communities can build the housing working families need.
- Protect renters, seniors, and mobile-home residents from displacement while expanding the overall housing supply.
- Promote pathways to homeownership so more working families can build financial security and put down roots in West Fresno County.
### Protect Farming, Water & Farm Jobs
- Fight for a reliable water supply for farmers, farmworkers, families, and rural communities.
- Protect agriculture from policies that threaten local farms and jobs and make sure West Fresno County has a strong voice in county and state decisions.
- Support family farms and agricultural businesses by improving infrastructure and cutting unnecessary red tape.
- Prepare the next generation for agriculture by expanding training in ag-tech, water management, equipment, and other modern agricultural careers.

## Campaign themes
#### Ballotpedia survey responses
See also: Ballotpedia's Candidate Connection
Lionel Lopez Jr. completed Ballotpedia's Candidate Connection survey in 2026. The survey questions appear in bold and are followed by Lopez's responses.
Expand All
Who are you? Tell us about yourself.
I am Lionel López, Jr., and I was born and raised in Parlier. Like most families here, we did not have much, and as a kid I picked grapes in the summers to help pay for school clothes. I attended Fresno State and worked as a community organizer, then spent years working construction in North Dakota, Montana and Texas before coming home. I have worked in construction since 2014, running job sites as a project manager, and today I own Lionel Lopez Construction, a licensed general contracting business. While I am running for office, I do not take or bid any construction work inside the City of Parlier. This community has given so much to me, and I am ready to give back.
Please list below 3 key messages of your campaign. What are the main points you want voters to remember about your goals for your time in office?
- Parlier’s economy should work for the people who already live and do business here. I will start by supporting the local businesses that have served our city for years and have received little help from City Hall. Then I will work to bring new businesses to Parlier so we can grow our tax base. A stronger tax base is how we pay for safe streets, parks that are cared for and a reliable water system without asking working families for more. Restoring our roots and growing into the future go together.
- Parlier’s money should be spent where residents can see it. The City has paid more than $800,000 to outside lawyers on two lawsuits, while families have received large catch-up water bills because the meter transmitters across town stopped working. As Mayor, I will bring the City’s finances to the public before decisions are made, push for a plan to close the general fund deficit, and fight for fair payment plans so residents are not punished for the City’s broken equipment.
- City Hall should listen before it decides. I first spoke before the Council because a group of respectful residents was dismissed when they raised a serious concern, and I have been showing up ever since. As Mayor, I will put community concerns on the agenda, explain City business in plain English and Spanish, and work with our police department and our neighbors so every family in Parlier feels safe. Leadership is a responsibility that should not be taken lightly, and I intend to measure up to its demands.
What areas of public policy are you personally passionate about?
Economic development, public safety, government transparency, and parks and recreation for our young people. I want to see a community sports facility in Parlier, with courts, an indoor gym and meeting space, so kids have somewhere to go after school and families have a place to gather. I also care deeply about water: clean, reliable service and fair, accurate billing for every household.
Who do you look up to? Whose example would you like to follow, and why?
I look up to Dr. Matthew Jendian, my mentor since I was a student at Fresno State. He founded the university’s Humanics Program, taught for more than thirty years, and now directs the Richter Center for Community Engagement and Service-Learning. His whole career has been about teaching students that education should be put to work for the community, through service, advocacy and community organizing. That lesson shaped me. It is why I went on to work as a community organizer, and it is why I believe a leader’s first job is to listen and bring people together. As Mayor, I will put community concerns on the agenda, explain City business in plain English and Spanish, and work with our police department and our neighbors so every family in Parlier feels safe. Leadership is a responsibility that should not be taken lightly, and I intend to measure up to its demands.
What areas of public policy are you personally passionate about?
Economic development, public safety, government transparency, and parks and recreation for our young people. I want to see a community sports facility in Parlier, with courts, an indoor gym and meeting space, so kids have somewhere to go after school and families have a place to gather. I also care deeply about water: clean, reliable service and fair, accurate billing for every household.
Who do you look up to? Whose example would you like to follow, and why?
I look up to Dr. Matthew Jendian, my mentor since I was a student at Fresno State. He founded the university’s Humanics Program, taught for more than thirty years, and now directs the Richter Center for Community Engagement and Service-Learning. His whole career has been about teaching students that education should be put to work for the community, through service, advocacy and community organizing. That lesson shaped me. It is why I went on to work as a community organizer, and it is why I believe a leader’s first job is to listen and bring people together. He still makes time for his former students, including me, and I want to lead Parlier the same way.
What characteristics or principles are most important for an elected official?

Next is the wisdom to tell the difference between what is good for the community and what is good for the official, because some leaders confuse their own success with the success of the group. Transparency matters just as much: when residents can see how decisions are made and where the money goes, a city is far less likely to be led astray. Finally, I believe leadership can be learned. It is a matter of willingness, and of showing up to do the work even when no one is watching.
What do you believe are the core responsibilities for someone elected to this office?
The Mayor runs the Council meetings and decides, with the Council, what comes before the public. That means the first responsibility is to put residents’ concerns on the agenda and give them a fair hearing. The Mayor also shares responsibility for the City’s budget, so every dollar should be spent carefully and explained openly. Most of all, the Mayor must listen to the people of Parlier, in English and in Spanish, and act on what he hears.

## Campaign themes
#### Ballotpedia survey responses
See also: Ballotpedia's Candidate Connection
Lionel Lopez Jr. completed Ballotpedia's Candidate Connection survey in 2026. The survey questions appear in bold and are followed by Lopez's responses.
Expand All
Who are you? Tell us about yourself.
I am Lionel López, Jr., and I was born and raised in Parlier. Like most families here, we did not have much, and as a kid I picked grapes in the summers to help pay for school clothes. I attended Fresno State and worked as a community organizer, then spent years working construction in North Dakota, Montana and Texas before coming home. I have worked in construction since 2014, running job sites as a project manager, and today I own Lionel Lopez Construction, a licensed general contracting business. While I am running for office, I do not take or bid any construction work inside the City of Parlier. This community has given so much to me, and I am ready to give back.
Please list below 3 key messages of your campaign. What are the main points you want voters to remember about your goals for your time in office?
- Parlier’s economy should work for the people who already live and do business here. I will start by supporting the local businesses that have served our city for years and have received little help from City Hall. Then I will work to bring new businesses to Parlier so we can grow our tax base. A stronger tax base is how we pay for safe streets, parks that are cared for and a reliable water system without asking working families for more. Restoring our roots and growing into the future go together.
- Parlier’s money should be spent where residents can see it. The City has paid more than $800,000 to outside lawyers on two lawsuits, while families have received large catch-up water bills because the meter transmitters across town stopped working. As Mayor, I will bring the City’s finances to the public before decisions are made, push for a plan to close the general fund deficit, and fight for fair payment plans so residents are not punished for the City’s broken equipment.
- City Hall should listen before it decides. I first spoke before the Council because a group of respectful residents was dismissed when they raised a serious concern, and I have been showing up ever since. As Mayor, I will put community concerns on the agenda, explain City business in plain English and Spanish, and work with our police department and our neighbors so every family in Parlier feels safe. Leadership is a responsibility that should not be taken lightly, and I intend to measure up to its demands.
What areas of public policy are you personally passionate about?
Economic development, public safety, government transparency, and parks and recreation for our young people. I want to see a community sports facility in Parlier, with courts, an indoor gym and meeting space, so kids have somewhere to go after school and families have a place to gather. I also care deeply about water: clean, reliable service and fair, accurate billing for every household.
Who do you look up to? Whose example would you like to follow, and why?
I look up to Dr. Matthew Jendian, my mentor since I was a student at Fresno State. He founded the university’s Humanics Program, taught for more than thirty years, and now directs the Richter Center for Community Engagement and Service-Learning. His whole career has been about teaching students that education should be put to work for the community, through service, advocacy and community organizing. That lesson shaped me. It is why I went on to work as a community organizer, and it is why I believe a leader’s first job is to listen and bring people together. He still makes time for his former students, including me, and I want to lead Parlier the same way.
What characteristics or principles are most important for an elected official?
Accountability comes first. An elected official must hold himself accountable to the people he serves, regardless of the consequences. Next is the wisdom to tell the difference between what is good for the community and what is good for the official, because some leaders confuse their own success with the success of the group. Transparency matters just as much: when residents can see how decisions are made and where the money goes, a city is far less likely to be led astray. Finally, I believe leadership can be learned. It is a matter of willingness, and of showing up to do the work even when no one is watching.
What do you believe are the core responsibilities for someone elected to this office?
The Mayor runs the Council meetings and decides, with the Council, what comes before the public. That means the first responsibility is to put residents’ concerns on the agenda and give them a fair hearing. The Mayor also shares responsibility for the City’s budget, so every dollar should be spent carefully and explained openly. Beyond that, the Mayor represents Parlier to the County, the State and anyone who might invest here, and should bring resources home. Most of all, the Mayor must listen to the people of Parlier, in English and in Spanish, and act on what he hears.
What legacy would you like to leave?
I would like to leave a Parlier that is financially stable, where the general fund is balanced and residents can see where every dollar goes. I want our local businesses to be stronger than when I started, and new ones to have chosen Parlier as their home. I would like the young people of this city to have a place of their own, a community sports facility where they can play, learn and stay out of trouble. Most of all, I want more residents involved in their city than ever before, so that good government in Parlier does not depend on any one person, including me.
What was your very first job? How long did you have it?
My first job was picking grapes in the summers as a kid, to help pay for my school clothes. I did that for every summer until I was 12. It was hard, hot work, and it taught me early what the families of Parlier do every day to provide for their children. I carry that with me, and it is a big part of why I am running.
What is something that has been a struggle in your life?
Like many people from Parlier, I had to leave home to find steady work. From 2013 to 2019 I worked construction in North Dakota, Montana and Texas, far from the community I love. Then, after I came back, COVID closed the testing centers just as I was preparing for my general contractor’s exam, and I had to wait years longer than I planned. I kept working, kept studying, and earned my license in 2026. Those years taught me patience and persistence, and they taught me that Parlier is where I belong.
A mayor is a leader in his or her city. What does that mean to you?
Being Mayor of Parlier is a responsibility, not a title, and it should not be taken lightly. To me, leadership means showing up, listening, and being honest with people even when the news is hard. It means explaining City business the way you would to a neighbor at the counter, not the way it reads on an agenda. It means bringing more people into the work, because a city where many residents see how things are done is a city that cannot easily be led astray. A leader earns respect and trust, and keeps them only so long as he continues to measure up to the demands of the job.
What do you perceive to be your city's greatest challenges over the next decade?
The first is money. Parlier is running a general fund deficit, and the City has spent more than $800,000 on outside lawyers for two lawsuits, so we must get our finances in order. The second is water. Broken meter transmitters across town have left families with large catch-up bills, and our water system needs reliable investment. The third is our tax base, which has stood still for too long. We need to support the businesses already here and attract new ones. The fourth is our young people, who need parks, programs and a reason to build their futures in Parlier instead of leaving the way I once had to.
What do you believe is the ideal relationship between the mayor's office and law enforcement?
The relationship should be built on support and accountability at the same time. Our officers deserve the resources, training and leadership they need to keep Parlier safe, and the City must budget honestly for them. In return, the public deserves transparency about how the department is run and how its money is spent. I want our police and our residents to know each other by name, through community policing and open communication, so that every family in Parlier, whatever their background, feels safe calling for help. The Mayor’s job is not to run the department, but to make sure it has what it needs and answers to the people it serves.
What organizations or individuals have endorsed your campaign?
Fresno County Democratic Party; Fresno County Democratic Women’s Club; Fresno-Madera-Tulare-Kings Central Labor Council, AFL-CIO; Assemblymember Esmeralda Soria; Matt Tuttle, Mayor of Reedley; Annalisa Perea, Fresno City Councilmember, District 1; Margaret Mims, retired Fresno County Sheriff and Supervisor-elect, District 4; Parlier Council Members Janie Molina (District 2), Kathy Solorio (District 3) and Diego Garza (District 4); Ismael Spindola, Parlier City Treasurer; Ruben Zarate, Chair of the Fresno County Democratic Party; Bob Perales, PAC Auto Center; Humberto Gomez; Raul Hinojosa; Daniel Collazo; and Parlier businesses Super Tacos, Arteaga Mexican Restaurant, Star 1 Gas, Beto’s Mexican Restaurant and State Foods Supermarket.
What was the first historical event that happened in your lifetime that you remember?
The first historical event I remember is the Challenger explosion on January 28, 1986. I was in third grade, and our whole school was packed into the resource room and the library to watch Christa McAuliffe become the first teacher in space. When the shuttle exploded, the entire room gasped. Some students started crying, and so did some of our teachers. The TV was turned off, the lights came on, and our teachers explained that a tragedy had happened, something no one had planned for. I still remember how quiet that room became. It was the first time I understood that the whole country could share the same moment of grief.

#### Campaign website
Lopez's campaign website stated the following:
# My Platform for Parlier
# Issues
Economic Development
Economic Growth
Parlier needs good-paying local jobs and a thriving small business community. I'll work to attract new employers, cut red tape for local entrepreneurs, and create programs that help small businesses grow and hire from within our community
Affordable Housing
Every Parlier family deserves a safe, affordable place to call home. I'll work with developers and housing agencies to expand affordable housing options while protecting the character of our neighborhoods.
Public Safety
Our Police Department
Every family in Parlier deserves to feel safe in their home and neighborhood. I'll work to bring more resources to our local police department, reduce emergency response times, and expand community policing programs that build trust between residents and officers.
Infrastructure
Our roads, parks, and water system need real investment. I'll prioritize fixing dangerous roads and improving our parks for families. And I will keep pressing on the water meters — residents should not be charged a flat rate for water that nobody is actually measuring.
Community Engagement
Youth & Senior Programs
Our kids are Parlier's future. I'll partner with local schools to expand after-school programs, create more opportunities for youth mentorship, and invest in safe spaces where young people can learn, play, and grow.
Transparency & Town Halls
Parlier residents deserve a City Hall that listens. I'll hold regular town halls, create open channels for community feedback, and restore transparency to local government — because trust is built one honest conversation at a time.
— Lionel Lopez Jr.'s campaign website (October 18, 2026)

## Campaign themes
#### Ballotpedia survey responses
See also: Ballotpedia's Candidate Connection
Lionel Lopez Jr. completed Ballotpedia's Candidate Connection survey in 2026. The survey questions appear in bold and are followed by Lopez's responses.
Expand All
Who are you? Tell us about yourself.
I am Lionel López, Jr., and I was born and raised in Parlier. Like most families here, we did not have much, and as a kid I picked grapes in the summers to help pay for school clothes. I attended Fresno State and worked as a community organizer, then spent years working construction in North Dakota, Montana and Texas before coming home. I have worked in construction since 2014, running job sites as a project manager, and today I own Lionel Lopez Construction, a licensed general contracting business. While I am running for office, I do not take or bid any construction work inside the City of Parlier. This community has given so much to me, and I am ready to give back.
Please list below 3 key messages of your campaign. What are the main points you want voters to remember about your goals for your time in office?
- Parlier’s economy should work for the people who already live and do business here. I will start by supporting the local businesses that have served our city for years and have received little help from City Hall. Then I will work to bring new businesses to Parlier so we can grow our tax base. A stronger tax base is how we pay for safe streets, parks that are cared for and a reliable water system without asking working families for more. Restoring our roots and growing into the future go together.
- Parlier’s money should be spent where residents can see it. The City has paid more than $800,000 to outside lawyers on two lawsuits, while families have received large catch-up water bills because the meter transmitters across town stopped working. As Mayor, I will bring the City’s finances to the public before decisions are made, push for a plan to close the general fund deficit, and fight for fair payment plans so residents are not punished for the City’s broken equipment.
- City Hall should listen before it decides. I first spoke before the Council because a group of respectful residents was dismissed when they raised a serious concern, and I have been showing up ever since. As Mayor, I will put community concerns on the agenda, explain City business in plain English and Spanish, and work with our police department and our neighbors so every family in Parlier feels safe. Leadership is a responsibility that should not be taken lightly, and I intend to measure up to its demands.
What areas of public policy are you personally passionate about?
Economic development, public safety, government transparency, and parks and recreation for our young people. I want to see a community sports facility in Parlier, with courts, an indoor gym and meeting space, so kids have somewhere to go after school and families have a place to gather. I also care deeply about water: clean, reliable service and fair, accurate billing for every household.
Who do you look up to? Whose example would you like to follow, and why?
I look up to Dr. Matthew Jendian, my mentor since I was a student at Fresno State. He founded the university’s Humanics Program, taught for more than thirty years, and now directs the Richter Center for Community Engagement and Service-Learning. His whole career has been about teaching students that education should be put to work for the community, through service, advocacy and community organizing. That lesson shaped me. It is why I went on to work as a community organizer, and it is why I believe a leader’s first job is to listen and bring people together. He still makes time for his former students, including me, and I want to lead Parlier the same way.
What characteristics or principles are most important for an elected official?
Accountability comes first. An elected official must hold himself accountable to the people he serves, regardless of the consequences. Next is the wisdom to tell the difference between what is good for the community and what is good for the official, because some leaders confuse their own success with the success of the group. Transparency matters just as much: when residents can see how decisions are made and where the money goes, a city is far less likely to be led astray. Finally, I believe leadership can be learned. It is a matter of willingness, and of showing up to do the work even when no one is watching.
What do you believe are the core responsibilities for someone elected to this office?
The Mayor runs the Council meetings and decides, with the Council, what comes before the public. That means the first responsibility is to put residents’ concerns on the agenda and give them a fair hearing. The Mayor also shares responsibility for the City’s budget, so every dollar should be spent carefully and explained openly. Beyond that, the Mayor represents Parlier to the County, the State and anyone who might invest here, and should bring resources home. Most of all, the Mayor must listen to the people of Parlier, in English and in Spanish, and act on what he hears.
What legacy would you like to leave?
I would like to leave a Parlier that is financially stable, where the general fund is balanced and residents can see where every dollar goes. I want our local businesses to be stronger than when I started, and new ones to have chosen Parlier as their home. I would like the young people of this city to have a place of their own, a community sports facility where they can play, learn and stay out of trouble. Most of all, I want more residents involved in their city than ever before, so that good government in Parlier does not depend on any one person, including me.
What was your very first job? How long did you have it?
My first job was picking grapes in the summers as a kid, to help pay for my school clothes. I did that for every summer until I was 12. It was hard, hot work, and it taught me early what the families of Parlier do every day to provide for their children. I carry that with me, and it is a big part of why I am running.
What is something that has been a struggle in your life?
Like many people from Parlier, I had to leave home to find steady work. From 2013 to 2019 I worked construction in North Dakota, Montana and Texas, far from the community I love. Then, after I came back, COVID closed the testing centers just as I was preparing for my general contractor’s exam, and I had to wait years longer than I planned. I kept working, kept studying, and earned my license in 2026. Those years taught me patience and persistence, and they taught me that Parlier is where I belong.
A mayor is a leader in his or her city. What does that mean to you?
Being Mayor of Parlier is a responsibility, not a title, and it should not be taken lightly. To me, leadership means showing up, listening, and being honest with people even when the news is hard. It means explaining City business the way you would to a neighbor at the counter, not the way it reads on an agenda. It means bringing more people into the work, because a city where many residents see how things are done is a city that cannot easily be led astray. A leader earns respect and trust, and keeps them only so long as he continues to measure up to the demands of the job.
What do you perceive to be your city's greatest challenges over the next decade?
The first is money. Parlier is running a general fund deficit, and the City has spent more than $800,000 on outside lawyers for two lawsuits, so we must get our finances in order. The second is water. Broken meter transmitters across town have left families with large catch-up bills, and our water system needs reliable investment. The third is our tax base, which has stood still for too long. We need to support the businesses already here and attract new ones. The fourth is our young people, who need parks, programs and a reason to build their futures in Parlier instead of leaving the way I once had to.
What do you believe is the ideal relationship between the mayor's office and law enforcement?
The relationship should be built on support and accountability at the same time. Our officers deserve the resources, training and leadership they need to keep Parlier safe, and the City must budget honestly for them. In return, the public deserves transparency about how the department is run and how its money is spent. I want our police and our residents to know each other by name, through community policing and open communication, so that every family in Parlier, whatever their background, feels safe calling for help. The Mayor’s job is not to run the department, but to make sure it has what it needs and answers to the people it serves.
What organizations or individuals have endorsed your campaign?
Fresno County Democratic Party; Fresno County Democratic Women’s Club; Fresno-Madera-Tulare-Kings Central Labor Council, AFL-CIO; Assemblymember Esmeralda Soria; Matt Tuttle, Mayor of Reedley; Annalisa Perea, Fresno City Councilmember, District 1; Margaret Mims, retired Fresno County Sheriff and Supervisor-elect, District 4; Parlier Council Members Janie Molina (District 2), Kathy Solorio (District 3) and Diego Garza (District 4); Ismael Spindola, Parlier City Treasurer; Ruben Zarate, Chair of the Fresno County Democratic Party; Bob Perales, PAC Auto Center; Humberto Gomez; Raul Hinojosa; Daniel Collazo; and Parlier businesses Super Tacos, Arteaga Mexican Restaurant, Star 1 Gas, Beto’s Mexican Restaurant and State Foods Supermarket.
What was the first historical event that happened in your lifetime that you remember?
The first historical event I remember is the Challenger explosion on January 28, 1986. I was in third grade, and our whole school was packed into the resource room and the library to watch Christa McAuliffe become the first teacher in space. When the shuttle exploded, the entire room gasped. Some students started crying, and so did some of our teachers. The TV was turned off, the lights came on, and our teachers explained that a tragedy had happened, something no one had planned for. I still remember how quiet that room became. It was the first time I understood that the whole country could share the same moment of grief.

#### Campaign website
Lopez's campaign website stated the following:
# My Platform for Parlier
# Issues
Economic Development
Economic Growth
Parlier needs good-paying local jobs and a thriving small business community. I'll work to attract new employers, cut red tape for local entrepreneurs, and create programs that help small businesses grow and hire from within our community
Affordable Housing
Every Parlier family deserves a safe, affordable place to call home. I'll work with developers and housing agencies to expand affordable housing options while protecting the character of our neighborhoods.
Public Safety
Our Police Department
Every family in Parlier deserves to feel safe in their home and neighborhood. I'll work to bring more resources to our local police department, reduce emergency response times, and expand community policing programs that build trust between residents and officers.
Infrastructure
Our roads, parks, and water system need real investment. I'll prioritize fixing dangerous roads and improving our parks for families. And I will keep pressing on the water meters — residents should not be charged a flat rate for water that nobody is actually measuring.
Community Engagement
Youth & Senior Programs
Our kids are Parlier's future. I'll partner with local schools to expand after-school programs, create more opportunities for youth mentorship, and invest in safe spaces where young people can learn, play, and grow.
Transparency & Town Halls
Parlier residents deserve a City Hall that listens. I'll hold regular town halls, create open channels for community feedback, and restore transparency to local government — because trust is built one honest conversation at a time.
— Lionel Lopez Jr.'s campaign website (October 18, 2026)

#### Campaign website
Ruiz's campaign website stated the following:
# My Campaign Pillars
Building a transparent, prosperous, and connected Sanger for every resident.
## City & School Collaboration
Our city and schools are deeply connected. Victor believes that when city leaders, schools, and residents work together, we can identify problems, listen to our community, and find solutions that make Sanger safer and stronger.
Victor is committed to building a stronger relationship between the City of Sanger and our schools, listening to students, families, educators, and community leaders and working together to address the issues that matter most.
Good leadership means listening, building relationships, and working together to get things done.
## Economic Development
A strong local economy starts with supporting the businesses, entrepreneurs, and families who call Sanger home. We will encourage smart, balanced growth, strengthen our downtown, and create opportunities for local businesses to succeed while preserving the character of our community.
## Transparent Finances
Responsible leadership starts with transparency. We are committed to open communication, accountable budgeting, and ensuring taxpayer dollars are managed wisely. Residents deserve clear information about city finances and confidence that decisions are being made with the community's long-term interests in mind.
— Victor Ruiz's campaign website (October 17, 2026)

#### Campaign website
Ruiz's campaign website stated the following:
# My Campaign Pillars
Building a transparent, prosperous, and connected Sanger for every resident.
## City & School Collaboration
Our city and schools are deeply connected. Victor believes that when city leaders, schools, and residents work together, we can identify problems, listen to our community, and find solutions that make Sanger safer and stronger.
Victor is committed to building a stronger relationship between the City of Sanger and our schools, listening to students, families, educators, and community leaders and working together to address the issues that matter most.
Good leadership means listening, building relationships, and working together to get things done.
## Economic Development
A strong local economy starts with supporting the businesses, entrepreneurs, and families who call Sanger home. We will encourage smart, balanced growth, strengthen our downtown, and create opportunities for local businesses to succeed while preserving the character of our community.
## Transparent Finances
Responsible leadership starts with transparency. We are committed to open communication, accountable budgeting, and ensuring taxpayer dollars are managed wisely. Residents deserve clear information about city finances and confidence that decisions are being made with the community's long-term interests in mind.
— Victor Ruiz's campaign website (October 17, 2026)

Selma Unified School District is a school district in California (Fresno County). During the 2025 school year, 5,914 students attended one of the district's 12 schools.
This page provides information regarding school board members, election rules, finances, academics, policies, and more details about the district.

Each year, state and local education agencies use tests and other standards to assess student proficiency. # Meet Scott Robertson
Scott Robertson is not a politician who shows up at election time. He is a Selma business owner, a neighbor, and a familiar face at the events that make this community special. You will find him rolling up his sleeves at downtown events, serving meals at the Christian Cafe, and showing up for the moments that matter most.
Alongside his wife Rose Gallardo, who has deep roots in Selma, he is connected to this community in a way that goes far beyond city hall. He listens. He shows up. And he genuinely cares about what is best for the people who call Selma home.
Over the past two years, Selma has built real momentum. Stronger finances, safer streets, and a city moving forward. That progress is worth protecting, and he is not about to let Selma lose the ground it has gained.
#### Experience That Delivers
#### Experience That Delivers
#### Experience That Delivers
With more than ten years on the Selma City Council, Scott Robertson knows how city government works and how to make it work better. His deep roots in public service and strong relationships across Fresno County mean Selma has a leader ready to deliver results from day one.
#### Fiscal Responsibility
#### Experience That Delivers
#### Experience That Delivers
Scott Robertson has spent over a decade fighting for every taxpayer dollar. As Mayor, he watches over every expenditure, asks the tough questions, and ensures Selma's budget works for the people who fund it and not for politics.
#### Public Safety
#### Experience That Delivers
#### Public Safety
Scott believes safe neighborhoods are the foundation of a strong community. From expanding downtown lighting to supporting police body cameras, he takes a proactive approach to keeping Selma's streets safe for families and businesses alike.
